attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own newsletter, written in his own voice.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'This is why' link back to models not knowing anything, the 'despite' investment framing, and the fingers/eyes/tools examples. Labelling it causal is right.

contract.note: Reading 'still fail' as 'commonly fail' is the ordinary reading. Narrowing 'do not know anything' to 'no learned grasp of physical structure' is a reasonable way to test a partly philosophical cause. It does not stretch the claim either way.

evidence.note: Nov 2023 paper, inside the period. Says diffusion models get finger counts and hand shapes wrong, and traces this to difficulty learning the physical structure of hands.
Feb 2024 OpenAI disclosure admitting Sora fails to treat a chair as a rigid object. It is the company describing itself, and it covers objects but not hands or eyes. Weak support.
March 2023 report that Midjourney v5 largely fixed hands but still made errors. Outside the target period, so it only modestly cuts against the claim.
March 2024 CVPR paper calling hand artifacts common. Just after the period, so context only, though it agrees with e1.

reviews.rationale: A paper from inside the period (e1) documents common hand errors and gives the structural-learning cause the contract tests. OpenAI's Sora page (e2) admits object failures. The Midjourney v5 improvement (e3) predates the period and still noted errors. Eyes are not directly evidenced. The deeper philosophical cause is not tested.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: Keeps the causal chain: staff replaced by AI, which led to fabricated and wrong stories, which ruined MSN. It drops the Bigfoot and traffic details, but these are not needed for the core claim.

contract.note: Reading 'destroyed' as ruined quality fits, since he cites current high traffic. Reading 'AI that posts' as automated curation is ordinary. The stolen, garbled stories were partner content that the automated system published, which the contract flags fairly.

evidence.note: Guardian, May 2020: Microsoft stopped using humans to select and edit MSN news and moved to automation.
CNN's Nov 2023 findings, quoted by Slashdot: people familiar with the site tie MSN's false and bizarre stories to relying on automation and AI instead of editors.
Futurism, quoted by Slashdot: MSN ran bogus Bigfoot stories after dropping its human editors.
Sept 2023: MSN distributed a plagiarized obituary full of errors from a partner site. Matches the stolen-and-wrong detail. Notes that Microsoft blamed a human for a separate error.

reviews.rationale: Reputable reporting shows all three parts the contract requires: Microsoft replaced its curators with automation, MSN then ran fabricated and plagiarized error-ridden stories, and sources tie the second to the first. The only counterpoint is Microsoft blaming a human for one error. 'Destroyed' is hyperbole, read as ruined quality.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: An unhedged statement about how the tools were at the time. 'May seem like the future' is a concession, not a hedge on the main point.

contract.note: The wording is vague. Reading it, through the next sentences, as unable to reliably produce a specific requested result (prompt-following, continuity) is an ordinary reading, not a stretched one.

evidence.note: Feb 2024 OpenAI disclosure: Sora may confuse spatial details, cause and effect, and camera paths given in a prompt. The company describing itself, but against its own interest.
Dec 2023 hands-on review: Pika 1.0 cannot guarantee continuity between clips and follows style requests poorly.
OpenAI's marketing claim of prompt adherence. It is self-description, not an evaluation, and the same page lists failures.

reviews.rationale: For the period, OpenAI's own disclosure lists Sora failing at specific prompt details, and a dated hands-on review finds Pika unreliable at continuity and style. The only evidence the other way is OpenAI's marketing line. The Sora evidence comes only from the developer, and a more positive Pika review went unread, so the support is thin but consistent.

attribution.note: Zitron's own gloss on McKinsey figures he cites. The sentence is his, though the data it interprets is McKinsey's.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'does not seem' hedge. It is a hedged interpretation of survey data and names no metric, population or threshold.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to supply a metric, population or threshold the speaker did not give, and treats the hedged gloss as unscorable.

reviews.rationale: 'Doesn't seem to be' is hedged wording, and under policy hedged claims are not scored. The sentence also gives no measure of 'generating money', no population and no period. The packet has no evidence items, and none would settle the claim without adding terms.
